# Modular Services

**Goal:** Define a service **once, as a module**, and run several named instances of it from `system.services.<name>`. Ship a portable core (`process.argv`, `configData`) that a non-systemd service manager could also consume, and keep systemd-specific settings behind a guard. Compose services from other services, including modules that packages export as `pkgs.<pkg>.services.default`. Know which parts are still moving, and the four traps that bite first.

Version note: modular services first shipped in **NixOS 25.11**. The 26.05 manual still marks them **"Status: in development … significant changes should be expected"**, and **user services are still "TBD"**. Everything below was evaluated against **nixos-26.05** (`26.05.20261008.7c8764b`) with **Nix 2.35.2**, and every unit file and error shown is real output from that evaluation. 26.05 adds two systemd-side options that 25.11 lacks, `systemd.mainExecStart` and `systemd.lib.escapeSystemdExecArgs`. Case 5 depends on them.

## Mental model

Classic NixOS services are **options in a module**: `services.nginx.enable = true` gives you exactly one nginx, configured through a fixed option tree. A modular service turns that inside out: the **service is the module**. You import it into a named slot as many times as you like, and each slot becomes its own unit.

```text
system.services.<name>  :: attrsOf (submodule, class "service")
        │
        ├── portable core (lib/services)          ← any service manager
        │     process.argv        command line, as a list (no shell)
        │     configData.<file>   text/source → path the manager exposes
        │     services.<sub>      sub-services this one owns
        │     meta.maintainers
        │
        └── systemd layer (nixos/modules/system/service/systemd)   ← NixOS only
              systemd.service      → systemd.services."<name>"
              systemd.services.<x> → extra units, prefixed with <name>
              systemd.socket(s)
              systemd.mainExecStart, systemd.lib.*   (26.05+)

NixOS realises it as:
  systemd.services.<name>                ExecStart from process.argv
  environment.etc."system-services/<name>/<file>"   from configData
  systemd.services.<name>-<sub>          for each sub-service
```

| Piece | What it means in practice |
|-------|---------------------------|
| `_class = "service"` | The module declares which evaluation it belongs to. Importing it anywhere else is an **error**, not a silent no-op (see The trap) |
| `process.argv` | A list, **not** a shell string. NixOS escapes it for systemd, so `%` and `$` reach the program literally |
| `configData.<file>.text` / `.source` | Files the service reads. On NixOS, `.path` resolves to `/etc/system-services/<name>/<file>` |
| `options ? systemd` | The portability guard. The systemd layer is present on NixOS and absent elsewhere |
| `services.<sub>` | Ownership, not ordering. A sub-service unit gets **no** `After=` on its parent unless you add it |
| NixOS defaults | `Type=simple`, `Restart=always`, `RestartSec=5`, `WantedBy=multi-user.target`, all overridable |
| Package-exported modules | `pkgs.<pkg>.services.default`, imported **inside** a `system.services.<name>` slot |

**When to use what** (26.05):

| Need | Prefer |
|------|--------|
| One instance of a mature service with a big option tree (nginx, postgres) | Classic `services.<x>` module |
| Several instances of the same thing with different settings | **Modular service**, one slot per instance |
| Your own small daemon, written once and reused across hosts or managers | **Modular service** with a portable core |
| A unit with no reuse value | Plain `systemd.services.<x>` (see *systemd via Nix*) |

## Worked examples

### Case 1: A portable service module

A status page: one static HTML file, served by `darkhttpd`. The page text and port are options. Nothing systemd-specific appears outside the guard.

```nix
# status-page.nix — a portable modular service: one static page, served by darkhttpd
# Non-module dependencies, passed with lib.modules.importApply
{ darkhttpd }:

# The service module
{ lib, config, options, ... }:
let
  cfg = config.statusPage;
in
{
  _class = "service";

  options.statusPage = {
    package = lib.mkOption {
      type = lib.types.package;
      default = darkhttpd;
      description = "Web server package.";
    };
    port = lib.mkOption {
      type = lib.types.port;
      description = "TCP port on 127.0.0.1.";
    };
    message = lib.mkOption {
      type = lib.types.str;
      default = "all systems nominal";
      description = "Text shown on the page.";
    };
  };

  config = {
    configData."index.html".text = ''
      <h1>${cfg.message}</h1>
    '';

    process.argv = [
      (lib.getExe cfg.package)
      (dirOf config.configData."index.html".path)
      "--port"
      (toString cfg.port)
      "--addr"
      "127.0.0.1"
    ];
  }
  // lib.optionalAttrs (options ? systemd) {
    # Only when the service manager is systemd (NixOS); ignored elsewhere.
    systemd.service.serviceConfig = {
      DynamicUser = true;
      Restart = "on-failure";       # the NixOS default is "always"
    };
  };
}
```

Three conventions here come straight from the nixpkgs contributor rules for modular services:

- **`importApply` for dependencies.** The file is a function that takes its packages (`{ darkhttpd }:`) and returns the module. The module itself never sees `pkgs`, because a service manager other than NixOS might not have one.
- **`configData` instead of `pkgs.writeText` plus a hard-coded path.** The service asks for a file, and the manager decides where it lives. `config.configData."index.html".path` is how the module finds out.
- **`lib.optionalAttrs (options ? systemd)` instead of `mkIf`.** `mkIf` would still need the `systemd` option to *exist*. The attribute-set guard avoids even mentioning it when it doesn't.

### Case 2: Two instances on one host

```nix
# flake.nix — one host, two instances of the same modular service
{
  inputs.nixpkgs.url = "github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-26.05";

  outputs = { nixpkgs, ... }: {
    nixosConfigurations.box = nixpkgs.lib.nixosSystem {
      modules = [
        ({ lib, pkgs, ... }:
          let
            statusPage = lib.modules.importApply ./status-page.nix {
              inherit (pkgs) darkhttpd;
            };
          in
          {
            nixpkgs.hostPlatform = "x86_64-linux";
            boot.isContainer = true;          # no bootloader/kernel needed for eval
            system.stateVersion = "26.05";

            system.services.status-public = {
              imports = [ statusPage ];
              statusPage.port = 8080;

              # a sub-service: TLS in front of the page, owned by status-public
              services.tls = {
                imports = [ pkgs.ghostunnel.services.default ];
                ghostunnel = {
                  listen = "0.0.0.0:8443";
                  target = "127.0.0.1:8080";
                  keystore = "/run/keys/status-public.pem";
                  disableAuthentication = true;
                };
              };
            };

            system.services.status-ops = {
              imports = [ statusPage ];
              statusPage.port = 8081;
              statusPage.message = "maintenance at 22:00 UTC";
            };
          })
      ];
    };
  };
}
```

`boot.isContainer = true` keeps this example evaluable without hardware configuration. On your lab host, add the two `system.services` blocks to the existing host module instead.

```bash
git add -A        # flakes only see tracked files
nix --version
nix eval --raw .#nixosConfigurations.box.config.system.nixos.version; echo
nix eval --json .#nixosConfigurations.box.config.systemd.services \
  --apply 's: builtins.filter (n: builtins.match "status-.*" n != null) (builtins.attrNames s)'; echo
nix eval --json .#nixosConfigurations.box.config.environment.etc \
  --apply 'e: builtins.filter (n: builtins.match "system-services/.*" n != null) (builtins.attrNames e)'; echo
```

```text
nix (Nix) 2.35.2
26.05.20261008.7c8764b
["status-ops","status-public","status-public-tls"]
["system-services/status-ops/index.html","system-services/status-public/index.html"]
```

One module gave **two** services plus a **third** unit for the sub-service, named `<parent>-<sub>`. Each instance has its own copy of `index.html` under `/etc/system-services/<name>/`.

### Case 3: Read the units NixOS generated

Evaluate the unit file without switching anything:

```bash
out=$(nix build --no-link --print-out-paths \
  '.#nixosConfigurations.box.config.systemd.units."status-ops.service".unit')
cat "$out/status-ops.service"
```

```text
[Unit]

[Service]
Environment="LOCALE_ARCHIVE=/nix/store/dc427sjs33dci797apv4lvsg1a69szn0-glibc-locales-2.42-100/lib/locale/locale-archive"
Environment="PATH=/nix/store/bhv6xyvqw6gjs3j488gi1z6wdv18bdpa-coreutils-9.11/bin:/nix/store/nl0wq6d4bpjrxmlax141liq0qr9z87gn-findutils-4.10.0/bin:/nix/store/cqhgy07rpxdwk9kd2qlc3cw4s9ajzm9f-gnugrep-3.12/bin:/nix/store/0s17nja4n8b63by0nlg1m31mxn2bq1g1-gnused-4.10/bin:/nix/store/kmzlca218j6j1ar292fxj7707qzypij8-systemd-260.5/bin:/nix/store/bhv6xyvqw6gjs3j488gi1z6wdv18bdpa-coreutils-9.11/sbin:/nix/store/nl0wq6d4bpjrxmlax141liq0qr9z87gn-findutils-4.10.0/sbin:/nix/store/cqhgy07rpxdwk9kd2qlc3cw4s9ajzm9f-gnugrep-3.12/sbin:/nix/store/0s17nja4n8b63by0nlg1m31mxn2bq1g1-gnused-4.10/sbin:/nix/store/kmzlca218j6j1ar292fxj7707qzypij8-systemd-260.5/sbin"
Environment="TZDIR=/nix/store/mkbbamycmw838fwxk21jz0nw3mhnmk16-tzdata-2026c/share/zoneinfo"
DynamicUser=true
ExecStart="/nix/store/qc2lzh2vk30sg00q6v08fd4gdl7mikmz-darkhttpd-1.17/bin/darkhttpd" "/etc/system-services/status-ops" "--port" "8081" "--addr" "127.0.0.1"
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
Type=simple

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

Read it against the module:

- `ExecStart` is `process.argv`, with every element quoted. The `configData` directory resolved to `/etc/system-services/status-ops`.
- `DynamicUser=true` and `Restart=on-failure` came from the guarded systemd block. Our `Restart` beat the NixOS default (`always`) without `mkForce`, because the systemd layer sets `Type`, `Restart`, `RestartSec` and `wantedBy` with `lib.mkDefault`.
- `RestartSec=5`, `Type=simple` and `WantedBy=multi-user.target` are NixOS's modular-service defaults.

Check the generated file, and smoke-test the server outside systemd:

```bash
page=$(nix build --no-link --print-out-paths \
  '.#nixosConfigurations.box.config.environment.etc."system-services/status-ops/index.html".source')
srv=$(nix build --no-link --print-out-paths \
  '.#nixosConfigurations.box.config.system.services.status-ops.statusPage.package')
mkdir -p /tmp/status-ops && install -m 644 "$page" /tmp/status-ops/index.html
"$srv/bin/darkhttpd" /tmp/status-ops --port 18081 --addr 127.0.0.1 >/dev/null & sleep 0.5
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18081/; kill %1
```

```text
<h1>maintenance at 22:00 UTC</h1>
```

Note that you can reach into an instance's options (`system.services.status-ops.statusPage.package`) like any other option path. That is handy in tests and `nix repl`.

### Case 4: A package-exported service as a sub-service

Packages can ship their own service module as `passthru.services.default`. In 26.05 the ones that do are `ghostunnel`, `git-pages`, `ktls-utils`, `php` and `snid` (25.11 had only `ghostunnel` and `php`). In Case 2, `status-public` imports ghostunnel as a **sub-service** to put TLS in front of the page:

```bash
out=$(nix build --no-link --print-out-paths \
  '.#nixosConfigurations.box.config.systemd.units."status-public-tls.service".unit')
cat "$out/status-public-tls.service"
```

```text
[Unit]
After=network.target
Wants=network.target

[Service]
Environment="LOCALE_ARCHIVE=/nix/store/dc427sjs33dci797apv4lvsg1a69szn0-glibc-locales-2.42-100/lib/locale/locale-archive"
Environment="PATH=/nix/store/bhv6xyvqw6gjs3j488gi1z6wdv18bdpa-coreutils-9.11/bin:/nix/store/nl0wq6d4bpjrxmlax141liq0qr9z87gn-findutils-4.10.0/bin:/nix/store/cqhgy07rpxdwk9kd2qlc3cw4s9ajzm9f-gnugrep-3.12/bin:/nix/store/0s17nja4n8b63by0nlg1m31mxn2bq1g1-gnused-4.10/bin:/nix/store/kmzlca218j6j1ar292fxj7707qzypij8-systemd-260.5/bin:/nix/store/bhv6xyvqw6gjs3j488gi1z6wdv18bdpa-coreutils-9.11/sbin:/nix/store/nl0wq6d4bpjrxmlax141liq0qr9z87gn-findutils-4.10.0/sbin:/nix/store/cqhgy07rpxdwk9kd2qlc3cw4s9ajzm9f-gnugrep-3.12/sbin:/nix/store/0s17nja4n8b63by0nlg1m31mxn2bq1g1-gnused-4.10/sbin:/nix/store/kmzlca218j6j1ar292fxj7707qzypij8-systemd-260.5/sbin"
Environment="TZDIR=/nix/store/mkbbamycmw838fwxk21jz0nw3mhnmk16-tzdata-2026c/share/zoneinfo"
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
DynamicUser=true
ExecStart="/nix/store/70zzr769qsi8jijkwjp2560f59p3fgg3-ghostunnel-1.8.4/bin/ghostunnel" "server" "--listen" "0.0.0.0:8443" "--target" "127.0.0.1:8080" "--disable-authentication" --keystore=${CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY}/keystore
LoadCredential=keystore:/run/keys/status-public.pem
Restart=always
RestartSec=5
Type=simple

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

The ghostunnel module did real systemd work: it loads the key through `LoadCredential=` and appends `--keystore=${CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY}/…` **unquoted**, so systemd expands the variable. That is the `mainExecStart` pattern from Case 5. Look at what is **missing**, though: there is no `After=status-public.service`. "Sub-service" means *owned by*, not *ordered after*. The manual says a sub-service relationship "does not automatically create any other relationship between services". Add the ordering yourself if the proxy should not start before its backend:

```nix
# order-fix.nix — make the TLS sub-service start after, and stop with, its parent
let
  flake = builtins.getFlake (toString ./.);
  sys = flake.nixosConfigurations.box.extendModules {
    modules = [{
      system.services.status-public.services.tls.systemd.service = {
        after = [ "status-public.service" ];
        bindsTo = [ "status-public.service" ];
      };
    }];
  };
  unit = sys.config.systemd.services.status-public-tls;
in { inherit (unit) after bindsTo; }
```

```bash
nix eval --impure --json --file order-fix.nix
```

```text
{"after":["status-public.service","network.target"],"bindsTo":["status-public.service"]}
```

In a real host, put those two lines directly into the `services.tls` block in `flake.nix`. `extendModules` is used here only so that the example can amend Case 2 without editing it.

### Case 5: systemd specifiers and variables (`mainExecStart`, 26.05+)

`process.argv` is portable, so NixOS escapes it completely: `%` becomes `%%` and `$` becomes `$$`. When you *want* systemd to substitute something (the unit name `%n`, a credentials directory, an environment variable), build `systemd.mainExecStart` from the escaped argv and append the unescaped part:

```nix
# trap-escape.nix — what happens to % and $ in process.argv
let
  flake = builtins.getFlake (toString ./.);
  sys = flake.nixosConfigurations.box.extendModules {
    modules = [
      ({ pkgs, ... }: {
        system.services.hello = {
          process.argv = [ "${pkgs.coreutils}/bin/echo" "unit=%n" "home=$HOME" ];
        };
        system.services.hello2 = { config, ... }: {
          process.argv = [ "${pkgs.coreutils}/bin/echo" ];
          systemd.mainExecStart =
            config.systemd.lib.escapeSystemdExecArgs config.process.argv
            + " unit=%n home=$HOME";
        };
      })
    ];
  };
in
map (n: "${n}: ${builtins.head sys.config.systemd.services.${n}.serviceConfig.ExecStart}")
  [ "hello" "hello2" ]
```

```bash
nix eval --impure --json --file trap-escape.nix | python3 -m json.tool
```

```text
[
    "hello: \"/nix/store/bhv6xyvqw6gjs3j488gi1z6wdv18bdpa-coreutils-9.11/bin/echo\" \"unit=%%n\" \"home=$$HOME\"",
    "hello2: \"/nix/store/bhv6xyvqw6gjs3j488gi1z6wdv18bdpa-coreutils-9.11/bin/echo\" unit=%n home=$HOME"
]
```

`hello` will print the literal text `unit=%n home=$HOME`. In `hello2`, systemd itself substitutes `%n` with the unit name (`hello2.service`) and expands `$HOME` from the service's environment when the unit starts. The first form is right for arguments that come from users or settings, because it can never be misinterpreted. Use the second only for the specific parts that need substitution, and only behind the `options ? systemd` guard, since other service managers have no `%n`.

## The trap

Four ways this goes wrong on a first attempt. All four were reproduced on 26.05.

**1. Importing a service module as a NixOS module.** Service modules go *inside* a `system.services.<name>` slot. Put one in the host's top-level `imports` (or `modules = [ … ]`) and the module system refuses:

```nix
# trap-class.nix — importing a service module as if it were a NixOS module
let
  flake = builtins.getFlake (toString ./.);
  pkgs = flake.inputs.nixpkgs.legacyPackages.x86_64-linux;
  sys = flake.nixosConfigurations.box.extendModules {
    modules = [ pkgs.ghostunnel.services.default ];
  };
in
sys.config.system.build.toplevel.drvPath
```

```bash
nix eval --impure --raw --file trap-class.nix 2>&1 | tail -n 6
```

```text
       error: The module `/nix/store/1ffpr0yhnxfkyj467rjjxfzsmc9564qb-source/pkgs/by-name/gh/ghostunnel/service.nix` (class: "service") cannot be imported into a module evaluation that expects class "nixos".

       Help:
       - Ensure that you are importing the correct module.
       - Verify that the module's `_class`, "service" matches the expected `class` "nixos".
       - If you are using a custom class, make sure it is correctly defined and used consistently across your modules.
```

That error is `_class` doing its job. Set `_class = "service"` in your own service modules too, so the same mistake fails loudly instead of quietly defining nonsense options.

**2. Expecting `%` or `$` in `process.argv` to be expanded.** Case 5: they are escaped. Use `systemd.mainExecStart` (26.05+). On 25.11 that option does not exist, and the workaround is a wrapper script.

**3. Overriding the package and getting the original binary.** A package-exported module may pin the package it came from in a way that ignores your override. In 26.05, `ghostunnel`'s `passthru.services.default` sets `ghostunnel.package = ghostunnel; # FIXME: finalAttrs.finalPackage`:

```nix
# trap-override.nix — a modular service from an overridden package
let
  flake = builtins.getFlake (toString ./.);
  sys = flake.nixosConfigurations.box.extendModules {
    modules = [
      ({ pkgs, ... }:
        let
          patched = pkgs.ghostunnel.overrideAttrs (old: {
            postInstall = (old.postInstall or "") + "\n# local patch\n";
          });
        in {
          system.services.gt = {
            imports = [ patched.services.default ];
            ghostunnel = {
              listen = "0.0.0.0:9443";
              target = "127.0.0.1:9000";
              keystore = "/run/keys/gt.pem";
              disableAuthentication = true;
            };
          };
          environment.etc."patched-ghostunnel".text = "${patched}";
        })
    ];
  };
in {
  patched = sys.config.environment.etc."patched-ghostunnel".text;
  used = sys.config.system.services.gt.ghostunnel.package.outPath;
}
```

```bash
nix eval --impure --json --file trap-override.nix | python3 -m json.tool
```

```text
{
    "patched": "/nix/store/bxmg1sxzfpbix6qh7fd9j9j4rdm5zig8-ghostunnel-1.8.4",
    "used": "/nix/store/70zzr769qsi8jijkwjp2560f59p3fgg3-ghostunnel-1.8.4"
}
```

The service imported from `patched` still runs the **unpatched** store path. Setting `ghostunnel.package = patched;` next to the import fails with "defined multiple times while it's expected to be unique", because the package's definition is a normal-priority value, not a default. You need `ghostunnel.package = lib.mkForce patched;`. With that line (and `lib` added to the module arguments), the same evaluation reports `"used": "/nix/store/bxmg1sxzfpbix6qh7fd9j9j4rdm5zig8-ghostunnel-1.8.4"`, the patched build. In your own packages, export services with `finalAttrs.finalPackage` so overrides flow through.

**4. Assuming sub-services are ordered.** Case 4: `status-public-tls` has no `After=` on `status-public`. Add `after`/`bindsTo` (or `requires`) explicitly when the relationship matters.

## Try this

1. Add a third instance, `status-staging`, on port 8082, with only two lines of new configuration. Confirm the new unit and `/etc` entry with the `nix eval` commands from Case 2.
2. Give `status-page.nix` a `statusPage.extraArgs` list option, append it to `process.argv`, and pass an argument containing `%`. Check the generated `ExecStart`, and explain why it is safe.
3. Rewrite `status-ops` to log its unit name at start-up using `systemd.mainExecStart` and `%n`. Keep it behind `options ? systemd`.
4. Write a NixOS VM test (`pkgs.testers.runNixOSTest`) that boots a node with `status-public` and `status-ops`, waits for both units, and `curl`s ports 8080 and 8081. The nixpkgs contributor guide requires such a test for every modular service in nixpkgs.
5. Port one of your own single-instance `systemd.services.<x>` definitions (from *systemd via Nix*) to a modular service. Which settings stayed portable, and which had to move behind the guard?

- nixpkgs contributor guide, `nixos/README-modular-services.md` (VM test, `meta.maintainers`, `options ? systemd`, `_class`, `finalAttrs.finalPackage`): <https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/blob/nixos-26.05/nixos/README-modular-services.md>
- Portable option declarations: <https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/blob/nixos-26.05/lib/services/service.nix>; systemd layer: <https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/blob/nixos-26.05/nixos/modules/system/service/systemd/service.nix>
- Original design and feedback thread, NixOS/nixpkgs PR #372170: <https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/372170>
- `ghostunnel` service module and package export (26.05): <https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/blob/nixos-26.05/pkgs/by-name/gh/ghostunnel/service.nix>
- systemd: `systemd.service(5)` *Command lines* and `systemd.unit(5)` *Specifiers*: <https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.service.html>
